clue.text: Most cryptic cipher in French that's carried by postman

parts.note: a cipher is a zero, which looks like the letter O

indicators.note: something carried by another is held inside it, so the postman's name goes around the French piece

parts.note: Postman Pat is the title character of a British children's TV series
the French for 'that' is que, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: A coded note inside a French letter makes the delivery man's load baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cipher' suggests a code, but it is a zero, O. Postman Pat is a British children's TV postman, and que is French for 'that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opaque means hard to see through or understand, and a cryptic thing is obscure, so the superlative forms match.

clue.text: On the cards provided by expert on a mix of tongues, Latin's above English

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert

indicators.note: in a down entry, above means placed before, so the Latin letter moves up to stand ahead of the English letter E

parts.note: Babel is the biblical tower where languages were confused
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A language expert's verdict on a hotch-potch of languages, with Latin ranked over English.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'above' means 'before', so 'above English' moves the Latin L ahead of the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the cards is likely to happen, the idiom matching an adjective of likelihood.

clue.text: Aussie tree as new, middle leaves sufficing

parts.note: qua is Latin for in the capacity of, as

indicators.note: the middle letter of the five-letter word leaves, so it is dropped

parts.note: doing can mean sufficing, as in that will be doing

explanation.surface: An Australian tree is like a new one, its central foliage being enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' suggests foliage on a tree, but it means 'goes away': the middle letter I leaves DOING, giving DONG.
explanation.definitionFit: This native Australian tree bears an edible fruit sometimes called the desert peach.

clue.text: Seventies rock band Queen dropping English tenor's vocal

parts.note: ELO, the Electric Light Orchestra, was a 1970s rock band

indicators.note: dropping means one letter of the band's name is left out

parts.note: Queen is used as written, as the name of the rock group
T is the standard abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: A Seventies band sacks its English tenor singer, leaving Queen behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' takes one E out of QUEEN, giving QUEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone vocal speaks out readily, and a fluent, articulate speaker is the same.

clue.text: Bunk off a rack even he felt should be repaired

indicators.note: repairing means putting the pieces back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a broken rack must be fixed before they skip work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'should be repaired' rearranges A RACK EVEN HE FELT. 'Bunk off' is British slang for skipping school or work.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for leaving without permission, much like skipping school or work.

clue.text: Elite force has revolutionary partizan step sideways, bottling it

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the run is read backwards
bottling means holding inside, so the run sits within the words partizan step sideways

explanation.surface: A rebel guerrilla sidesteps, losing his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottling it' finds ZANSTEPS in PARTIZAN STEP SIDEWAYS and 'revolutionary' turns it round. 'Bottling it' also suggests losing one's nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Russian special forces units are an elite military corps.

clue.text: Rising after one match is over, with nil to each side

indicators.note: after puts the rest of the wordplay following the numeral

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: to each side means the word for nil sits on both sides of the turned word

parts.note: nada is Spanish-derived slang for nothing

indicators.note: is over means turned over, so the word for match is read backwards

parts.note: to fit is to match

explanation.surface: After a game ends level at nil-nil, unrest breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' and 'over' suggest a game ending, but FIT is read backwards and 'to each side' wraps NADA (Spanish nothing) round it.
explanation.definitionFit: An Arabic word for the Palestinian uprisings, so a revolt or rebellion.

clue.text: Put something vocal into practice? Yes and no!

definitions.text: Put something vocal into practice? Yes and no!

parts.words: Put something vocal into practice? Yes and no!
parts.note: yes: to sing or speak in unison is to put something vocal into use; no: the reverse operation, practice (USE) put into something vocal (CHORD), builds the word

explanation.walkthrough: The reading goes both ways: 'Put something vocal into practice' defines it, and the reverse, USE (practice) inside CHORD (something vocal), builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sing or say together is to give voice in unison, putting a vocal piece into use.

clue.text: Answer I'm very much obliged to steal should need arise

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you
to pinch is to steal in informal speech

explanation.surface: Someone thanks a benefactor profusely while planning to rob them if the chance comes.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for 'thanks'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for in an emergency or if necessary, matching the conditional sense of the clue phrase.

clue.text: Track wild koala bears over watering hole

indicators.note: bears means carries or holds, so the railway-and-koala string holds a letter inside it

parts.note: RY is short for railway, a kind of track

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of the word koala run loose into a new order

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A trail of an untamed marsupial leads across to a drinking pool in the bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals again, but means 'holds'. The Royal Oak is one of Britain's commonest pub names.
explanation.definitionFit: Watering hole is slang for a pub, and this is a very common English pub name.

clue.text: Hire-rate fluctuates: more or less like 25?

indicators.note: a rate that fluctuates moves up and down, so these letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Hire charges go up and down, more or less in line with something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fluctuates' rearranges HIRERATE. 25 is ERDGEIST, an earth-spirit, so something more like it is more of the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-reference is to an earth-spirit, so being more like one means being more of the soil, a comparative of earthy.

clue.text: It's in hairdo: sufficient for GP to be brought in?

definitions.text: It's in hairdo: sufficient for GP to be brought in?

parts.note: a DA (duck's arse) is a slicked-back 1950s men's hairstyle

indicators.note: something brought in is placed inside the other pieces, so the doctor goes into the hairstyle-plus-slang string

parts.note: nuff is slang for enough
a GP is a family doctor, abbreviated DR

explanation.surface: A hair problem bad enough that a doctor needs calling in.
explanation.walkthrough: A DA (duck's arse) is a greased-back 1950s men's hairstyle, and a scalp complaint might well send one to the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Scurf flakes lodged in a hairstyle, a condition someone might consult a doctor about, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Africans stick in right solution

indicators.note: in places the stick inside the right-plus-solution pair

parts.note: ANS is short for answer, a solution
a wand is a thin stick

explanation.surface: People from a continent put a stick into the correct liquid mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' suggests a liquid, but it is an answer, abbreviated ANS.
explanation.definitionFit: People from the central African republic of Kigali are inhabitants of one African nation, so Africans.

clue.text: Bedfordshire station's audience's slow to respond in quiz by day

indicators.note: what an audience hears is speech, so the phrase is taken by its sound

parts.note: a slow contestant is late on the buzzer

explanation.surface: A local radio station's listeners are too slow pressing the buzzer in a daytime quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audience's' says 'late on buzzer' is heard; it sounds like the first part of the town's name. Leighton Buzzard is a market town in Bedfordshire, England, with a railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: The town in that English county has a mainline railway stop, so it names a station there.

clue.text: Delivery for one brother involved in escape

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped inside, so these letters go into the word for escape

parts.note: a leak is an escape of gas or liquid
e.g. means for example, for one

explanation.surface: A sibling is caught up in a jailbreak, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' puts EGBR inside LEAK after its L. A leg break is a kind of ball bowled in cricket, and 'delivery' is a cricket ball bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bowled ball is called a delivery, and this is one spinning from the leg side.

clue.text: Leader in adversity, one roundly rejecting U turns

definitions.text: Leader in adversity, one roundly rejecting U turns

indicators.note: turns means the letters are rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: rejecting means one letter of roundly is thrown out

explanation.surface: A prime minister in hard times famously refused to make a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' drops U from ROUNDLY and 'turns' shuffles RONDLY with A (from 'Leader in adversity'). Margaret Thatcher, the Iron Lady, said 'The lady's not for turning'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, famed for refusing to back down.

clue.text: Margo O'Donnell does apply

definitions.meaning: the singer's name has the run G O O D across its two words (marGO O'Donnell), so it contains that word for virtuous
to apply is to be relevant or remain in force, as a rule does

explanation.walkthrough: Margo O'Donnell is an Irish country singer; her name contains GOOD running across its two words, so it literally holds that word.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain valid or true, as a rule does when it applies.

clue.text: Lorraine's a bird being pulled? Lord, no!

parts.note: in Lorraine, a French region, the word for a is un
a tit is a small songbird
led means drawn along, as a horse is led

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a woman called Lorraine is being chatted up.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorraine looks like a woman's name, but it is the French region, so its 'a' is UN. 'Bird' and 'pulled' are British slang for a woman and getting a date.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is not a lord has no noble rank, so is without a title.

clue.text: Airline business looking up, covering miles before we land

indicators.note: before places the first part ahead of the closing pronoun
covering means wrapping around, so the turned word goes round the miles and airline letters
looking up in a down entry means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: biz is informal for business
BA is British Airways

explanation.surface: An airline's trade is improving, flying many miles before touchdown.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'looking up' means read upwards, i.e. backwards; MBA is not intended, the M and BA come from separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: A country in southern Africa, so a land or nation.

clue.text: Scoundrel boxes (seconds out), winds up using teeth

parts.note: a rat is a scoundrel or traitor

indicators.note: seconds out means one S, for second, is taken out

parts.note: chests are large boxes

explanation.surface: A villain fights, the boxing referee calls seconds out, and he gets wound up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds out' is the call clearing a boxer's helpers from the ring; here it removes an S from CHESTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothed wheel with a pawl lets something turn one way only, as in winding mechanisms.

clue.text: Stew's eaten hot and is not as gruesome

indicators.note: is not as tells the solver to put the letters is where as stood
something eaten goes inside the eater, so the hot letter goes into the stew

parts.note: goulash is a Hungarian stew

explanation.surface: A stew has been eaten hot and is not as revolting as before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten' puts H into GOULASH; 'is not as' swaps the AS for IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghoulish describes a morbid, grisly delight in death, a close synonym of horrid.

clue.text: Libertarian put his own first and charity second

definitions.text: Libertarian put his own first and charity second

indicators.note: the libertarian's own first letter is taken, which begins the word

parts.note: aid is help given in charity
to second a proposal is to back it

explanation.surface: A free-market thinker looks after himself before giving to good causes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: a libertarian is relaxed about rules, and the wordplay puts the word's own first letter first, then AID, then BACK.
explanation.definitionFit: A libertarian takes a relaxed, hands-off view of rules, so easygoing fits the whole description.

clue.text: Send down and make short work of mourner in class

indicators.note: in places the shortened poem inside the class

parts.note: a rate is a grade or class

indicators.note: making a word short means docking its last letter

parts.note: an elegy is a poem of mourning

explanation.surface: Dismiss someone and cut short a grieving person's time in a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send down' also means to expel from university, but here it is to move a team to a lower league.
explanation.definitionFit: To relegate is to demote, as a football team is moved down a division.

clue.text: Poster campaigner's no women's make-up specialist?

parts.note: an ad is a poster or advertisement
a women's libber is a feminist campaigner; drop women's and libber remains

explanation.surface: A protest poster says the activist is no expert in women's cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics, but it means making things up on the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who improvises speech is skilled at inventing lines, a playful sense of making things up.

clue.text: Redhead in early eighties with very poor curls

parts.note: and can mean with, as in ham and eggs

indicators.note: curls means the letters twist into a different order

explanation.surface: A ginger-haired person in the early 1980s with badly done curls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curls' rearranges VPOOR into ROPOV. 'Redhead' means a Soviet (Red) leader: Yuri Andropov led the USSR from 1982 to 1984.
explanation.definitionFit: A Red is a communist, and this Soviet general secretary headed the USSR from 1982 to 1984.

clue.text: Earth-spirit: it is like a God, free wheeling, regularly

indicators.note: wheeling means turning round, so the picked letters are read backwards
regularly means taking every other letter of the phrase it is like a God free

parts.words: it is like a God, free

explanation.surface: Something godlike rolls freely, again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of IT IS LIKE A GOD FREE, giving TSIEGDRE, and 'wheeling' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: German for earth plus spirit: the spirit of the earth summoned in Goethe's Faust.
